demos.objective: Recognize how data is organized in everyday situations
demos.slide: syn-s02: slide 2 of 7; slide 2 of 3 in seg-01
demos.chunks:
[syn-s02-c1] (syn-s02) Outline | - Organizing data | - Object basics
[syn-p01-c1] (reference) People organize information all the time so it is quick to use. A music playlist keeps songs in a chosen order. People waiting at a bus stop board in the order they arrived. The undo button in a text editor removes the most recent change first.
demos.script: Let’s start with how we organize things every day. A music playlist keeps songs in the order you pick, so you can play them fast. People at a bus stop get on in the same order they arrived. And when you hit undo in a text editor, it takes away the last change first. All of these are ways we arrange information so it’s easy to use.

demos.objective: Explain encapsulation and access control in a class
demos.slide: syn-s07: slide 7 of 7; slide 1 of 1 in seg-05
demos.chunks:
[syn-s07-c1] (syn-s07) Encapsulation | - Keep data and methods together | - Hide the data inside the class | - Use it through public methods
[syn-p05-c1] (reference) Encapsulation puts an object's data and the methods that use that data together in one class, and keeps the data from being changed directly from outside. In Java the fields are usually declared private, and other code works with the object through public methods.
[syn-p05-c3] (reference) A vending machine is a good picture of encapsulation. Buyers use only the buttons and the coin slot. The coin counter and the motors stay inside the case, and the owner can replace them without changing how buyers use the machine.
demos.script: Okay, so encapsulation is like putting a fence around an object's data and the code that works with it. This keeps the data safe inside the class, so nothing outside can change it directly. Instead, other code has to use public methods—kind of like how you can't reach into a vending machine to grab snacks, but you can press buttons to get what you want. The machine's inner parts stay hidden, just like the private fields in a class.

demos.question: Which collection does not allow duplicate items?
demos.options:
A: Bag
B: Set
C: List
D: Stack
demos.misconception: Bag rejects duplicates: Believes a bag keeps only one copy of each item.
demos.chunks:
[syn-s05-c1] (syn-s05) Collections | - Bag | - Set | - List | - Stack | - Queue | - Map
[syn-p03-c2] (reference) A bag holds items in no particular order and allows duplicates. A set holds items in no particular order and does not allow duplicates. A list keeps items in a sequence, and each item has a position.
demos.title: When a collection allows duplicates
demos.text: A lot of you picked bag, thinking it rejects duplicates. But the lesson says a bag actually lets you add the same item more than once. The slide lists the collections, and only set is the one that keeps just one copy of each item. So bag is not the answer.
